title: Currency Arbitrage Optimization using Quantum Annealing, QAOA and Constraint Mapping
abstract_summary: This preprint formulates currency arbitrage as a combinatorial optimization problem (QUBO and NchooseK) and implements solutions using D-Wave quantum annealing and gate-based QAOA (Qiskit), including an NchooseK-based mapping for the D-Wave Ocean suite. Comparative experiments on small currency sets show D-Wave annealers converged to optimal arbitrage cycles more reliably, while the QAOA implementation in simulation struggled with constraint satisfaction and parameter optimization, highlighting current limitations and avenues for future work.
methodology_description: The authors formulate the currency-arbitrage problem as a combinatorial optimization over a directed graph (nodes = currencies, directed edges = exchange rates). They convert multiplicative profits into additive costs using the negative logarithm of exchange rates and introduce binary decision variables bij that indicate inclusion of each directed edge. Constraints enforcing exactly one incoming and one outgoing edge per currency are encoded as penalty terms, yielding a QUBO objective Ctot = sum(-log(rij) bij) + mp * penalty. They implement three solution routes: (1) Quantum annealing via D-Wave: the QUBO (built with dimod) is submitted through D-Wave’s EmbeddingComposite sampler / Leap service (Advantage V4.1) and also via an NchooseK formulation solved with the D-Wave Ocean solver; (2) Mapping the same QUBO into IBM Qiskit native format and solving with a QAOA ansatz (4 layers) implemented in Qiskit v1.2.0, using COBYLA (SciPy) for classical parameter optimization and AerSimulator for execution; (3) A constraint-programming translation using the NchooseK DSL where hard nck constraints enforce row/column selection (one outgoing/one incoming) and soft constraints bias selection toward high-profit edges via repeated soft-constraint weights proportional to -log(rij). Postprocessing maps returned bitstrings to closed currency cycles and computes profit rates (product of rates), and experiments compare solution quality, degeneracy of minimum-energy solutions, and frequencies across shots and configurations.
experimental_setup: Small synthetic exchange-rate tables of size 4, 5 and 6 currencies. D-Wave Advantage V4.1 via Leap (EmbeddingComposite sampler) and Ocean solvers for annealing; NchooseK formulation run against Ocean solver; QAOA implemented in Qiskit v1.2 and executed on AerSimulator (noiseless), with classical optimization by COBYLA.
dataset_used: Small currency exchange-rate tables used in experiments: a 4-currency table (EUR, USD, CHF, JPY) taken from prior work (Tatsumura et al. [2]) and additional 5- and 6-currency exchange-rate matrices supplied in the paper. These are small synthetic/illustrative matrices (4x4, 5x5, 6x6) of pairwise exchange rates.

experiment_input.source: Exchange-rate tables provided in the paper (Table I, II, III); Table I referenced from Tatsumura et al. [2].
experiment_input.preprocessing: Converted rates rij to costs via -log(rij). Constructed binary decision variables bij for each directed edge. Built QUBO dictionary with linear cost terms and quadratic penalty terms enforcing one incoming and one outgoing edge per node. For NchooseK, constructed hard nck constraints per row/column and soft constraints with weights proportional to -log(rij) (repeated according to a scaling factor).

pipeline_steps: Formulate graph and variables bij; compute cost C = sum(-log(rij) bij) and penalty P enforcing exactly one incoming and one outgoing edge per node; form Ctot = C + mp * P.
QUBO construction: encode Ctot into a QUBO dictionary (dimod).
D-Wave quantum annealing: submit QUBO via EmbeddingComposite sampler on D-Wave Leap (Advantage V4.1). Run with 1,000 shots; postprocess lowest-energy samples to extract cycles and compute profit.

NchooseK route: express hard nck constraints for rows/columns; add soft constraints with weights derived from -log(rij) repeated according to a scaling factor; solve with D-Wave Ocean solver (also with 1,000 shots, anneal time 200 microseconds), repeat experiments (6 runs reported).

QAOA route: translate QUBO to Qiskit native format; build QAOA ansatz with p=4 layers; run variational loop using COBYLA (SciPy) to optimize 2*p parameters (gamma, beta); execute final circuit on AerSimulator with 1,024 shots; postprocess measured bitstrings into cycles and profit.
experiment_process.parameters_and_iterations: D-Wave/NchooseK: 1,000 shots per run; annealing time 200 microseconds (NchooseK Ocean solver); soft constraint scaling factor = 100; repeated 6 times for stability. QAOA: p = 4 layers; COBYLA optimizer (required ~92 iterations to converge; optimization run up to ~100 iterations); AerSimulator with 1,024 shots. Circuit statistics: 30 qubits, circuit depth (critical path) 44, total gates 234 (about half two-qubit). Optimal found QAOA parameters (γ, β) listed per layer.

experiment_output.result_format: Binary bitstrings representing selected edges (bij) which are post-processed into closed currency cycles (sequences of currencies).
experiment_output.metrics_reported: Profit rate (product of exchange rates along cycle, reported as >1 profitable or <1 loss), lowest-energy frequency counts (degenerate minima frequency across shots), cycle path strings, final objective value for QAOA (example: -29.242109307796706).
experiment_output.baselines_and_comparisons: Comparison across D-Wave QUBO solver, NchooseK Ocean solver, NchooseK Qiskit solver, and QAOA (Qiskit AerSimulator). Table IV reports best-found cycles and profit rates for each method and problem size.

hardware_details.gate_hardware_attempted: IBM quantum devices mentioned as target, but main reported execution was on AerSimulator
hardware_details.other_tools: dimod, NchooseK DSL, SciPy (COBYLA), D-Wave Ocean

reproducibility_notes: The paper provides detailed algorithmic descriptions (QUBO formulation, cost: -log(rij), penalty structure, and parameter settings) and explicit small exchange-rate matrices (4-, 5-, 6-currency examples). It states software and versions used (Qiskit v1.2.0, D-Wave Ocean, dimod, AerSimulator, SciPy COBYLA) and reports solver parameters (shots, anneal time, scaling). However, no public code repository or explicit link to code/data release is provided in the preprint. Reproduction would require re-implementing the QUBO/NchooseK encoding and parameter tuning; access to D-Wave Leap or equivalent annealer and to Qiskit/AerSimulator is required.

[supported] D-Wave quantum annealing (via the QUBO solver) produced profitable arbitrage cycles for 4, 5 and 6 currency examples in the authors' experiments (profit rates > 1 in several cases).

[supported] The NchooseK formulation mapped the problem into hard (exact-one-in-row/column) and soft (profit-bias) constraints and was solvable via D-Wave’s Ocean solver; degenerate minimum-energy solutions were observed but the optimal solution was contained in the solution set.
[supported] QAOA implemented with Qiskit (simulator) failed to satisfy the cycle constraints in the presented experiments and returned suboptimal/trivial solutions for the small examples tested.

[supported] NchooseK (Ocean solver) solutions showed increasing degeneracy and reduced fraction of shots giving the exact optimal path as the number of currencies increased, though the fraction of profitable ( >1 ) cycles among degenerate minima increased with problem size.
[supported] The authors provide explicit QAOA parameters (γ and β) for their 4-layer run (numerical values reported).

[speculative] The paper claims that NchooseK provides a notable enhancement over current QAOA frameworks (statement made without a thorough quantitative cross-platform benchmarking demonstrating consistent improvement).

[speculative] The authors suggest that evolutionary/global optimizers (e.g., differential evolution) used in related VQE work could improve QAOA parameter optimization and overcome local minima issues in future work.

results_summary: The authors recast currency arbitrage as a QUBO and implemented three solution approaches: D-Wave quantum annealing (direct QUBO), an NchooseK constraint formulation solved via D-Wave’s Ocean solver, and a gate-based QAOA implementation using Qiskit. In their small-scale experiments (4–6 currencies) the D-Wave annealer reliably produced profitable cycles (profit >1) and converged rapidly to low-energy solutions. The NchooseK approach produced degenerate minimum-energy solutions but included the optimal cycles among them; degeneracy grows with problem size. QAOA runs on the Qiskit simulator struggled to meet the combinatorial cycle constraints and returned suboptimal solutions, and the circuit compiled to substantial width/depth (30 qubits, depth 44, 234 gates), which the authors argue is challenging for current noisy hardware. The paper documents practical implementation details (shots, anneal times, optimizer behavior) and highlights limitations in scaling, optimizer convergence, and constraint handling.

quantum_advantage_detail: The paper compares quantum annealing and gate-based QAOA implementations for small arbitrage instances and finds D-Wave annealing more effective in these tests, but it does not claim or demonstrate a quantum advantage over classical algorithms. The reported comparisons are between quantum platforms/encodings and are limited to small problem sizes without benchmarking against classical solvers or asymptotic speedup claims.
limitations: QUBO formulation is mathematically sophisticated and not intuitive, and solution quality is sensitive to choices like number of shots and penalty (mp) weighting (author-stated).
QAOA experienced poor convergence with the classical optimizer (COBYLA), getting trapped in local minima and producing suboptimal solutions in simulation (author-stated).
QAOA had difficulty satisfying problem constraints (under both NchooseK and standard formulations) and produced solutions that omitted required edges (author-stated).

NchooseK formulation yields degenerate minimum-energy solutions driven by soft-constraint penalties, making it harder to reliably extract the unique optimal arbitrage path as problem size grows (author-stated).
Annealing results exhibited increased degeneracy and fewer optimal-shot occurrences as the number of currencies increased (author-stated).

Circuit complexity for QAOA is high (example: 30 qubits, depth 44, ~234 gates with many two-qubit gates), making execution on current noisy hardware error-prone due to decoherence and gate errors (author-stated).
Running QAOA on real quantum hardware is constrained by device noise and the lack of practical error correction, limiting practical performance (author-stated).
Mapping/embedding QUBO problems onto D-Wave hardware requires careful/optimal embedding to mitigate errors; mapping is non-trivial (author-stated).
Limited experimental scale: experiments were only run on 4, 5, and 6 currencies due to computational resource constraints (author-stated).
[inferred] Scalability concerns: the approaches (both annealing and gate-based) may not scale practically to realistic, larger currency universes without significant algorithmic or hardware advances.

[inferred] Real-world trading frictions (transaction costs, spreads, slippage, latency, and liquidity constraints) were not modeled, so the reported profits may not translate to executable strategies.

[inferred] Using static exchange-rate snapshots ignores the time-sensitive and dynamic nature of arbitrage opportunities (market rates change rapidly), raising questions about real-time applicability.
[inferred] The need to hand-tune soft-constraint scaling and other hyperparameters implies sensitivity and potential non-robustness of the method across datasets/environments.

[inferred] Limited evaluation metrics: the study emphasizes solution quality (profit) but provides limited quantitative comparison of runtime, end-to-end latency, or resource usage relevant to trading use-cases.

key_ideas: #idea:near-term-feasibility — D-Wave quantum annealer (Advantage V4.1) reliably found optimal arbitrage cycles on small 4–6 currency instances, suggesting practical near-term applicability of annealing for small combinatorial finance problems.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Gate-based QAOA implemented in Qiskit (p=4) struggled in simulation with constraint satisfaction and parameter optimization, indicating current variational approaches face difficulties even on small structured instances.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Hybrid workflow used: classical preprocessing (cost transform -log(rij)), classical optimizers (COBYLA) to tune QAOA parameters, and classical postprocessing to extract cycles from bitstrings, highlighting practical hybrid QPU-CPU patterns.

#idea:hybrid-approach — NchooseK constraint-mapping (hard nck constraints plus soft-weighted edges) for D-Wave demonstrates value of problem-specific constraint encodings and hybrid solver features to enforce combinatorial structure.
contradictions: contradiction:scalability — The paper reports that QAOA (p=4) on noiseless simulator failed to robustly satisfy constraints and find optimal cycles, contradicting optimistic claims that variational gate-based approaches are currently scalable/practical for structured combinatorial finance problems; instead the annealer solved small instances more reliably.
